title: Coherence Estimation Beyond the Liouvillian Gap in a Finite Nonequilibrium System
authors: Sonali Brahma, Trishna Kalita, Himangshu Prabal Goswami
abstract: We investigate the estimation of bath-induced coherence in a finite quantum system interacting with thermal reservoirs. Enhancement of coherence estimation is transient and the estimation precision totally disappears at the steady state despite the system retaining finite coherence. By analyzing the full Liouvillian eigenspectrum, we demonstrate that the optimal sensing window emerges from the competition between identifiable contributory modes' temporal relaxation and statistical importance. Neither is the linear inverse scaling of Liouvillian gap with transient optimal time a signature of unimodal contribution to optimal sensing, nor is the existence of multimodal dynamics a signature of nonlinear scaling. The inverse Liouvillian gap does not obey any general scaling with the optimal sensing time of coherence and we prove our numerical results analytically using a general Markovian framework. We further show that coupling the finite system to a quantum cavity and maintaining a thermal bias, transforms the transient metrological optimization into a sustained steady-state resource.
summary: The paper rigorously investigates coherence estimation in complex, non-equilibrium quantum systems, showing that simple scaling laws based on the Liouvillian gap are insufficient. By analyzing the full spectral decomposition of the QFIM, the authors prove that optimal sensing depends on a balance between mode relaxation and statistical weight. This work establishes new criteria for understanding metrological resources in open quantum dynamics.
main_problem: The study investigates how to accurately estimate bath-induced coherence (BIC) in a finite, non-equilibrium quantum system when the estimation precision is limited by dynamics beyond what is predicted by the simple Liouvillian gap.
main_result: Optimal coherence estimation time does not generally scale simply with the inverse of the Liouvillian gap; instead, it depends on the competition between the statistical weight and temporal relaxation rates of multiple contributing eigenmodes. Furthermore, coupling to a cavity can transform transient metrology into a sustained steady-state resource.
method: The authors analyze the time evolution of the Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM) by performing spectral decomposition of the density matrix using the full Liouvillian eigenspectrum.
model_or_system: The model is an open quantum V-type system interacting with thermal reservoirs (hot and cold baths), governed by a Markovian master equation ($\dot{ho} = Lho$). The analysis extends to include coupling with a quantum cavity.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM) elements, coherence parameters ($p_c, p_h$), and the optimal interrogation time ($t^*$).
important_parameters: Liouvillian gap ($\Delta$), reservoir temperatures ($T_h, T_c$), and modal expansion coefficients ($c_n$) vs. relaxation rates ($\lambda_n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Born–Markov approximation to derive the master equation; spectral decomposition is used to separate temporal (Liouvillian) and statistical contributions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the open system, time evolution of density matrix elements showing coherence survival, and plots comparing QFI vs. rescaled time for different temperatures, alongside optimal time vs. inverse Liouvillian gap.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical model and observables (BIC, QFI). It then critiques the standard reliance on $\propto 1/\Delta$ scaling. The core is a detailed spectral analysis showing that transient optimization depends on mode competition, culminating in demonstrating how cavity coupling can stabilize this resource.
why_interesting: This work provides crucial theoretical insight into quantum metrology limits for open systems, moving beyond simplified gap estimates to account for the full complexity of non-equilibrium dynamics and multi-mode contributions, which is highly relevant for designing robust quantum sensors.
